title: Machine learning finds plasma protein signals up to 14 years before Parkinson diagnosis
summary: Using UK Biobank measurements of 2,937 plasma proteins, researchers found 446 dysregulated proteins in incident Parkinson cases and used machine learning to select a 23-protein panel for prediction. The panel achieved test AUCs of 0.78 in incident and 0.795 in prevalent cases; nine selected proteins were already dysregulated 10–14 years before diagnosis. In a separate Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative cohort, a 16-protein subset shared between platforms achieved validation AUC up to 0.76.
ai_technology: Support vector machine and other machine-learning models, with recursive feature elimination for panel selection
organization: Johnson & Johnson; UK Biobank; Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative collaborators

evidence.tested: Using UK Biobank measurements of 2,937 plasma proteins, researchers found 446 dysregulated proteins in incident Parkinson cases and used machine learning to select a 23-protein panel for prediction.
evidence.unknown: The result is a retrospective biomarker/prediction study, not a validated screening test or evidence that intervention based on the panel improves outcomes. The external PPMI analysis retrained and tested models in that cohort rather than evaluating a frozen UK Biobank model; validation AUCs varied by visit definition, and the reported maximum was 0.76. Protein associations and co-expression modules do not establish causal mechanisms. It is distinct from the earlier 2024 iRBD study in this ledger (DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-48961-3): separate cohorts and a different 23-protein/14-year result versus an eight-protein targeted panel and up-to-seven-year conversion finding; this record does not claim first discovery of presymptomatic plasma signals in Parkinson disease.
evidence.ai_role: Machine-learning classifiers were trained on UK Biobank plasma proteomic measurements to predict incident Parkinson disease; recursive feature elimination selected a 23-protein subset. The authors then tested the shared protein subset in the separate PPMI cohort using its own train/test split.
